UNC3886 has used a PowerShell script to search memory dumps for credentials.

techniques.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
techniques.procedure: UNC3886 has executed Windows commands on guest virtual machines through `vmtoolsd.exe`.

techniques.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell
techniques.procedure: UNC3886 has used a bash script to install malicious vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs).
UNC3886 has used Python scripts to enumerate ESXi hosts and guest VMs.

techniques.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Hypervisor CLI
techniques.procedure: UNC3886 has used the esxcli command line utility to modify firewall rules, install malware, and for artifact removal.
UNC3886 has exploited zero-day vulnerability CVE-2023-20867 to enable execution of privileged commands across Windows, Linux, and PhotonOS (vCenter) guest VMs.
UNC3886 has used the the esxcli command line to remove files created by malicious vSphere Installation Bundles from disk.
UNC3886 has used scripts to timestomp ESXi hosts prior to installing malicious vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs).

techniques.technique_name: Indicator Removal: Clear Network Connection History and Configurations
techniques.procedure: UNC3886 has cleared specific events that contained the threat actor’s IP address from multiple log sources.
UNC3886 has staged captured credentials in `var/log/ldapd.2.gz`.
UNC3886 has used tools to hijack valid SSH accounts.
UNC3886 has harvested and used vCenter Server service accounts.
UNC3886 has used `vmtoolsd.exe` to enumerate files on guest machines.
UNC3886 has deployed backdoors that communicate over TCP to compromised network devices and over VMCI to ESXi hosts.
UNC3886 has used installation scripts to collect the system time on targeted ESXi hosts.
UNC3886 has exploited CVE-2022-42475 in FortiOS SSL VPNs to obtain access.
UNC3886 has exoloited CVE-2023-34048 to enable command execution on vCenter servers and CVE-2023-20867 in VMware Tools to execute unauthenticated Guest Operations from ESXi hosts to guest VMs.
UNC3886 has used the TABLEFLIP traffic redirection utility to listen for specialized command packets on compromised FortiManager devices.
UNC3886 maintained persistence on FortiGate Firewalls through ICMP port knocking.
UNC3886 exploited CVE-2022-22948 in VMware vCenter to obtain encrypted credentials from the vCenter postgresDB.
UNC3886 has used rundll32.exe to execute MiniDump for dumping LSASS process memory.

techniques.technique_name: Server Software Component: vSphere Installation Bundles

techniques.technique_name: Credentials from Password Stores: Password Managers
techniques.procedure: UNC3886 has targeted KeyPass password database files for credential access.

UNC3886 has utilzed Python scripts to transfer files between ESXi hosts and guest VMs.
UNC3886 has deployed custom malware families on Fortinet and VMware systems.

UNC3886 has tampered with and disabled logging services on targeted systems.

groups.name: Velvet Ant
groups.description: Velvet Ant is a threat actor operating since at least 2021. Velvet Ant is associated with complex persistence mechanisms, the targeting of network devices and appliances during operations, and the use of zero day exploits.

techniques.procedure: Velvet Ant has transferred tools within victim environments using SMB.

techniques.technique_name: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
techniques.procedure: Velvet Ant used a malicious DLL, `iviewers.dll`, that mimics the legitimate "OLE/COM Object Viewer" within Windows.

techniques.technique_name: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: RC Scripts
techniques.procedure: Velvet Ant used a modified `/etc/rc.local` file on compromised F5 BIG-IP devices to maintain persistence.
Velvet Ant has used a custom tool, "VELVETTAP", to perform packet capture from compromised F5 BIG-IP devices.
Velvet Ant used the `wmiexec.py` tool within Impacket for remote process execution via WMI.
Velvet Ant has enumerated existing network connections on victim devices.
Velvet Ant initial execution included launching multiple `svchost` processes and injecting code into them.

techniques.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell
techniques.procedure: Velvet Ant used a custom tool, VELVETSTING, to parse encoded inbound commands to compromised F5 BIG-IP devices and then execute them via the Unix shell.
Velvet Ant has used reverse SSH tunnels to communicate to victim devices.
Velvet Ant accessed vulnerable Cisco switch devices using accounts with administrator privileges.
Velvet Ant has enumerated local files and folders on victim devices.
Velvet Ant has tunneled traffic from victims through an internal, compromised host to proxy communications to command and control nodes.
Velvet Ant sent commands to compromised F5 BIG-IP devices in an encoded format requiring a passkey before interpretation and execution.
Velvet Ant has leveraged access to internet-facing remote services to compromise and retain access to victim environments.

Velvet Ant exploited CVE-2024-20399 in Cisco Switches to which the threat actor was already able to authenticate in order to escape the NX-OS command line interface and gain access to the underlying operating system for arbitrary command execution.
Velvet Ant executed and installed PlugX as a Windows service.
Velvet Ant transferred files laterally within victim networks through the Impacket toolkit.
Velvet Ant has used random high number ports for PlugX listeners on victim devices.
Velvet Ant has used a reverse SSH shell to securely communicate with victim devices.
Velvet Ant has used malicious DLLs executed via legitimate EXE files through DLL search order hijacking to launch follow-on payloads such as PlugX.
Velvet Ant attempted to disable local security tools and endpoint detection and response (EDR) software during operations.
Velvet Ant modified system firewall settings during PlugX installation using `netsh.exe` to open a listening, random high number port on victim devices.

groups.description: VOID MANTICORE is a threat group assessed to operate on behalf of Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). Active since at least mid-2022, VOID MANTICORE has targeted government entities, critical infrastructure, and private sector organizations across Albania, Israel, and the United States. VOID MANTICORE conducts destructive cyber operations, combining wiper attacks with hack-and-leak campaigns. The group has operated under multiple public-facing personas, including HomeLand Justice in operations against Albania, Karma and Karma Below in campaigns targeting Israeli organizations, and Handala Hack, its current primary persona, which has claimed activity against Israeli and U.S. entities, including a March 2026 attack against Stryker Corporation. VOID MANTICORE has been observed collaborating with Scarred Manticore, which has been linked to initial access operations preceding VOID MANTICORE’s activity.

groups.description: Volt Typhoon is a People's Republic of China (PRC) state-sponsored actor that has been active since at least 2021, primarily targeting critical infrastructure organizations in the US and its territories including Guam. Volt Typhoon's targeting and pattern of behavior have been assessed as pre-positioning to enable lateral movement to operational technology (OT) assets for potential destructive or disruptive attacks. Volt Typhoon has emphasized stealth in operations using web shells, living-off-the-land (LOTL) binaries, hands on keyboard activities, and stolen credentials.. The group has leveraged compromised SOHO routers to proxy command and control traffic and obscure its infrastructure, activity associated with the KV botnet.. Reporting indicates a separate initial access cluster, SYLVANITE, has been observed exploiting internet-facing edge devices and transferring access to Volt Typhoon, also tracked as VOLTZITE, for follow-on operations.

WIRTE has collected documents from victims' email accounts.
WIRTE has used Base64 to decode malicious VBS script.
WIRTE has used links embedded in emails to lure users into downloading malicious files.
WIRTE has attempted to lure users into opening malicious documents including MS Word and Excel files, at times using a decoy document to encourage execution of malicious payloads.
WIRTE has used `regsvr32.exe` to trigger the execution of a malicious script.
WIRTE has configured C2 servers to check location and user-agent strings for victim endpoints to prevent sending a payload to sandboxed environments.
WIRTE has sent emails to intended victims with malicious MS Word and Excel attachments.
WIRTE has sent targeted spearphishing emails with malicious links directing victims to malware downloads.
WIRTE has used HTTPS over ports 2083 and 2087 for C2.
WIRTE has used RAR archives containing a legitimate executable and a lure document to execute malicious DLLs via sideloading.
WIRTE has registered domains designed to mimic legitimate sites for use in phishing campaigns.
WIRTE has used compromised emails, including one belonging to an Israel-based technology reseller, to deliver targeted spearphishing messages.
WIRTE has obtained and used Empire and Rclone for post-exploitation activities.
WIRTE has directed victims to malicious payloads staged on file sharing services.
WIRTE has used utilized look-alike domains and graphics of trusted security solution providers to entice victims to click on phishing links.

groups.name: Wizard Spider
groups.description: Wizard Spider is a Russia-based financially motivated threat group originally known for the creation and deployment of TrickBot since at least 2016. Wizard Spider possesses a diverse arsenal of tools and has conducted ransomware campaigns against a variety of organizations, ranging from major corporations to hospitals.

techniques.procedure: Wizard Spider has dumped the lsass.exe memory to harvest credentials with the use of open-source tool LaZagne.

techniques.technique_name: OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager
techniques.procedure: Wizard Spider has acquired credentials from the SAM/SECURITY registry hives.

Wizard Spider has gained access to credentials via exported copies of the ntds.dit Active Directory database. Wizard Spider has also created a volume shadow copy and used a batch script file to collect NTDS.dit with the use of the Windows utility, ntdsutil.
Wizard Spider has collected data from a compromised host prior to exfiltration.

Wizard Spider has used ipconfig to identify the network configuration of a victim machine. Wizard Spider has also used the PowerShell cmdlet `Get-ADComputer` to collect IP address data from Active Directory.

Wizard Spider has used networkdll for network discovery and psfin specifically for financial and point of sale indicators. Wizard Spider has also used AdFind, `nltest/dclist`, and PowerShell script Get-DataInfo.ps1 to enumerate domain computers, including the domain controller.
Wizard Spider has used the WebDAV protocol to execute Ryuk payloads hosted on network file shares.
Wizard Spider has used RDP for lateral movement and to deploy ransomware interactively.
Wizard Spider has used SMB to drop Cobalt Strike Beacon on a domain controller for lateral movement.
Wizard Spider has used Window Remote Management to move laterally through a victim network.

techniques.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Command Obfuscation
techniques.procedure: Wizard Spider used Base64 encoding to obfuscate an Empire service and PowerShell commands.
Wizard Spider has used "whoami" to identify the local user and their privileges.

Wizard Spider has used scheduled tasks to install TrickBot, using task names to appear legitimate such as WinDotNet, GoogleTask, or Sysnetsf. It has also used common document file names for other malware binaries.
Wizard Spider has exfiltrated domain credentials and network enumeration information over command and control (C2) channels.
Wizard Spider has used WMI and LDAP queries for network discovery and to move laterally. Wizard Spider has also used batch scripts to leverage WMIC to deploy ransomware.

techniques.technique_name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
techniques.procedure: Wizard Spider has exfiltrated victim information using FTP.
Wizard Spider has used scheduled tasks to establish persistence for TrickBot and other malware.
Wizard Spider has used process injection to execute payloads to escalate privileges.
Wizard Spider has injected malicious DLLs into memory with read, write, and execute permissions.
Wizard Spider has used macros to execute PowerShell scripts to download malware on victim's machines. It has also used PowerShell to execute commands and move laterally through a victim network.

techniques.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
techniques.procedure: Wizard Spider has used `cmd.exe` to execute commands on a victim's machine.
Wizard Spider has used file deletion to remove some modules and configurations from an infected host after use.
Wizard Spider has used HTTP for network communications.
Wizard Spider has collected and staged credentials and network enumeration information, using the networkdll and psfin TrickBot modules.
Wizard Spider has staged ZIP files in local directories such as, `C:\PerfLogs\1\` and `C:\User\1\` prior to exfiltration.
Wizard Spider has used valid credentials for privileged accounts with the goal of accessing domain controllers.
Wizard Spider has used administrative accounts, including Domain Admin, to move laterally within a victim network.

Wizard Spider has used Systeminfo and similar commands to acquire detailed configuration information of a victim's machine. Wizard Spider has also utilized the PowerShell cmdlet `Get-ADComputer` to collect DNS hostnames, last logon dates, and operating system information from Active Directory.

Wizard Spider has identified domain admins through the use of `net group "Domain admins" /DOMAIN`. Wizard Spider has also leveraged the PowerShell cmdlet `Get-ADComputer` to collect account names from Active Directory data.
Wizard Spider can transfer malicious payloads such as ransomware to compromised machines.

Wizard Spider has modified the Registry key `HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest` by setting the `UseLogonCredential` registry value to `1` in order to force credentials to be stored in clear text in memory. Wizard Spider has also modified the WDigest registry key to allow plaintext credentials to be cached in memory.
Wizard Spider has accessed victim networks by using stolen credentials to access the corporate VPN infrastructure.
Wizard Spider has used the “net view” command to locate mapped network shares.
Wizard Spider has created local administrator accounts to maintain persistence in compromised networks.
Wizard Spider has created and used new accounts within a victim's Active Directory environment to maintain persistence.
Wizard Spider has used batch scripts that utilizes WMIC to execute a BITSAdmin transfer of a ransomware payload to each compromised machine.
Wizard Spider has lured victims into clicking a malicious link delivered through spearphishing.
Wizard Spider has lured victims to execute malware with spearphishing attachments containing macros to download either Emotet, Bokbot, TrickBot, or Bazar.
Wizard Spider has exploited or attempted to exploit Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472) and EternalBlue (MS17-010) vulnerabilities.
Wizard Spider has utilized `rundll32.exe` to deploy ransomware commands with the use of WebDAV.

techniques.technique_name: File and Directory Permissions Modification: Windows Permissions
techniques.procedure: Wizard Spider has used the icacls command to modify access control to backup servers, providing them with full control of all the system folders.
Wizard Spider has used taskkill.exe and net.exe to stop backup, catalog, cloud, and other services prior to network encryption.
Wizard Spider has used WMIC and vssadmin to manually delete volume shadow copies. Wizard Spider has also used Conti ransomware to delete volume shadow copies automatically with the use of vssadmin.
Wizard Spider has used WMI to identify anti-virus products installed on a victim's machine.
Wizard Spider has utilized the PowerShell script `Get-DataInfo.ps1` to collect installed backup software information from a compromised machine.

techniques.technique_name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
techniques.procedure: Wizard Spider has installed TrickBot as a service named ControlServiceA in order to establish persistence.

techniques.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
techniques.procedure: Wizard Spider has established persistence via the Registry key `HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run` and a shortcut within the startup folder.

techniques.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Winlogon Helper DLL
techniques.procedure: Wizard Spider has established persistence using Userinit by adding the Registry key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon.

techniques.technique_name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash
techniques.procedure: Wizard Spider has used the `Invoke-SMBExec` PowerShell cmdlet to execute the pass-the-hash technique and utilized stolen password hashes to move laterally.
Wizard Spider has used PowerShell cmdlets `Get-GPPPassword` and `Find-GPOPassword` to find unsecured credentials in a compromised network group policy.
Wizard Spider has used Digicert code-signing certificates for some of its malware.

techniques.technique_name: Credentials from Password Stores: Windows Credential Manager
techniques.procedure: Wizard Spider has used PowerShell cmdlet `Invoke-WCMDump` to enumerate Windows credentials in the Credential Manager in a compromised network.

techniques.technique_name: Adversary-in-the-Middle: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
techniques.procedure: Wizard Spider has used the Invoke-Inveigh PowerShell cmdlets, likely for name service poisoning.

techniques.technique_name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting
techniques.procedure: Wizard Spider has used Rubeus, MimiKatz Kerberos module, and the Invoke-Kerberoast cmdlet to steal AES hashes.

techniques.technique_name: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility
techniques.procedure: Wizard Spider has archived data into ZIP files on compromised machines.
Wizard Spider has used spearphishing attachments to deliver Microsoft documents containing macros or PDFs containing malicious links to download either Emotet, Bokbot, TrickBot, or Bazar.
Wizard Spider has sent phishing emails containing a link to an actor-controlled Google Drive document or other free online file hosting services.

techniques.technique_name: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
techniques.procedure: Wizard Spider has exfiltrated stolen victim data to various cloud storage providers.

Wizard Spider has used `services.exe` to execute scripts and executables during lateral movement within a victim's network. Wizard Spider has also used batch scripts that leverage PsExec to execute a previously transferred ransomware payload on a victim's network.
Wizard Spider has used stolen credentials to copy tools into the `%TEMP%` directory of domain controllers.
Wizard Spider has leveraged ProtonMail email addresses in ransom notes when delivering Ryuk ransomware.

Wizard Spider has utilized tools such as Empire, Cobalt Strike, Cobalt Strike, Rubeus, AdFind, BloodHound, Metasploit, Advanced IP Scanner, Nirsoft PingInfoView, and SoftPerfect Network Scanner for targeting efforts.
Wizard Spider has obtained code signing certificates signed by DigiCert, GlobalSign, and COMOOD for malware payloads.
Wizard Spider has shut down or uninstalled security applications on victim systems that might prevent ransomware from executing.

groups.name: ZIRCONIUM
groups.description: ZIRCONIUM is a threat group operating out of China, active since at least 2017, that has targeted individuals associated with the 2020 US presidential election and prominent leaders in the international affairs community.

techniques.procedure: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to query the Registry for proxy settings.
ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to enumerate proxy settings in the target environment.

techniques.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing
techniques.procedure: ZIRCONIUM has used multi-stage packers for exploit code.
ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to capture the username on a compromised host in order to register it with C2.
ZIRCONIUM has spoofed legitimate applications in phishing lures and changed file extensions to conceal installation of malware.
ZIRCONIUM has created a run key named `Dropbox Update Setup` to mask a persistence mechanism for a malicious binary.
ZIRCONIUM has exfiltrated files via the Dropbox API C2.

techniques.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
techniques.procedure: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to open a Windows Command Shell on a remote host.
ZIRCONIUM has used Python-based implants to interact with compromised hosts.
ZIRCONIUM has exploited CVE-2017-0005 for local privilege escalation.
ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to capture the processor architecture of a compromised host in order to register it with C2.

ZIRCONIUM has utilized an ORB (operational relay box) network – consisting compromised devices such as small office and home office (SOHO) routers, IoT devices, and leased virtual private servers (VPS) – to proxy traffic.
ZIRCONIUM has used Dropbox for C2 allowing upload and download of files as well as execution of arbitrary commands.
ZIRCONIUM has used tools to download malicious files to compromised hosts.
ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to capture the time on a compromised host in order to register it with C2.
ZIRCONIUM has used the AES256 algorithm with a SHA1 derived key to decrypt exploit code.
ZIRCONIUM has used malicious links in e-mails to lure victims into downloading malware.
ZIRCONIUM has used the msiexec.exe command-line utility to download and execute malicious MSI files.

techniques.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
techniques.procedure: ZIRCONIUM has created a Registry Run key named `Dropbox Update Setup` to establish persistence for a malicious Python binary.

techniques.technique_name: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
techniques.procedure: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to steal credentials from installed web browsers including Microsoft Internet Explorer and Google Chrome.
ZIRCONIUM has used malicious links in e-mails to deliver malware.

techniques.technique_name: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
techniques.procedure: ZIRCONIUM has exfiltrated stolen data to Dropbox.
ZIRCONIUM has used AES encrypted communications in C2.
ZIRCONIUM has purchased domains for use in targeted campaigns.
ZIRCONIUM has used GitHub to host malware linked in spearphishing e-mails.
ZIRCONIUM has compromised network devices such as small office and home office (SOHO) routers and IoT devices for ORB (operational relay box) Proxy networks.
ZIRCONIUM targeted presidential campaign staffers with credential phishing e-mails.
ZIRCONIUM has used web beacons in e-mails to track hits to attacker-controlled URL's.

ZIRCONIUM has utilized an ORB (operational relay box) network – consisting compromised devices such as small office and home office (SOHO) routers, IoT devices, and leased virtual private servers (VPS) – to obfuscate the origin of C2 traffic.
